opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually one of the most important things we look for, and it's a bit counterintuitive, because people assume we'd just want the most technically brilliant mathematicians we can find. Of course rigor and depth matter a lot. But what we're doing at Axiom is quite new. We're asking mathematicians to work alongside AI systems, to think about formalization in Lean, to care about how a proof gets represented so a machine can verify it, and sometimes to accept that a model might find an approach they wouldn't have considered.

If someone comes in with a very fixed view, like "real mathematics is only done with pen and paper," or "AI will never contribute anything meaningful to research," it becomes very hard to collaborate. They won't engage with what the system is actually doing, and they won't give the kind of feedback that helps us improve it. The mathematicians who do really well with us are curious. They're willing to say, "Okay, this is strange, but let me understand why the model did this." They're willing to change their workflow and learn new tools, even when they're already very accomplished in their field.

There's also a cultural side. We bring together people from very different backgrounds: pure mathematicians, people who think about formal verification, machine learning researchers, engineers. Each group has its own language and its own idea of what counts as a good result. Open-mindedness is what lets those groups actually talk to each other instead of talking past each other. A mathematician has to respect that an engineer's concern about scalability is a real concern, and an ML researcher has to respect that a mathematician's sense of what's elegant or important carries a lot of wisdom.

And honestly, the field is moving so fast that whatever we believe today about what AI can or can't do in mathematics may be wrong in six months. So we need people who can update their beliefs, who hold their views with some humility. That's what lets a team keep learning together, and I think that ends up mattering more than any single credential.

r001.rationale: The response mentions engineers’ concerns about scalability and mathematicians’ fixed views about pen-and-paper mathematics, but it does not attribute opposition to scaling to a conception of mathematics as a craft.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, open-mindedness is probably the trait I weigh most heavily, and it comes from a very practical place rather than a philosophical one.

What we're doing at Axion is trying to build AI that can do real mathematics, and that means asking people who have spent their entire careers thinking in one particular way to suddenly collaborate with a system that thinks very differently. A traditional mathematician is trained to be skeptical, to distrust anything that isn't a complete, rigorous argument. That skepticism is valuable, I want to keep it. But if someone walks in already convinced that a machine can never have a genuine mathematical idea, they will never actually look carefully at what the model produces. They'll dismiss the interesting partial insights along with the noise, and we lose the signal.

The people who thrive with us are the ones who can hold two things at once. They can say, "This output is wrong," and in the same breath say, "But there's something here, let me understand why it went in this direction." That curiosity about failure modes, about a different kind of reasoning, is what lets us improve the system and also what sometimes leads to new mathematics we wouldn't have found on our own.

There's also a cultural reason. Mathematics has quite rigid hierarchies, who's at which institution, who studied under whom, which subfield is considered deep. At Axion we have people coming from pure math, from software engineering, from physics, from machine learning, and we need them to actually listen to each other. The combinatorialist has to take the engineer's intuition about the training pipeline seriously, and the engineer has to be patient when the number theorist says the proof isn't a proof yet. If people arrive with the attitude that their way of seeing is the only valid one, the collaboration simply doesn't work.

So when I interview someone, I'm less interested in whether they can solve the problem I give them and more interested in how they react when I show them an approach they haven't seen before. Do they get defensive, or do they lean in? That tells me almost everything.

r001.rationale: The response describes skepticism toward machine-generated mathematical ideas, but does not mention opposition to scaling or attribute it to a view of mathematics as a craft.

astra-6.text:
I think open-mindedness matters because being good at solving a problem isn’t always the same as being willing to rethink how you’re approaching it. You can be technically very strong, but if you’re too attached to one method, you might miss a useful idea from someone who thinks differently.

When hiring mathematicians at Axion, I’d look for that combination of rigor and curiosity: can you defend your reasoning, but also change your mind when someone makes a better argument? Can you explore an unfamiliar approach without dismissing it immediately? That makes collaboration much more productive, especially when you’re working on questions where nobody knows the right approach yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open-mindedness, collaboration, and unfamiliar approaches, but does not attribute anyone’s opposition to scaling to a conception of mathematics as a craft.

sol-6.1.text: I think open-mindedness matters because mathematical ability alone doesn’t tell you how someone will approach an unfamiliar problem. You need to be willing to say, “I don’t know,” try a different perspective, and take someone else’s idea seriously—even when it challenges your own. That’s especially important when people are working together: you want the conversation to help everyone get closer to an answer, rather than become a contest over who’s right.
